answer:
Recent studies show microplastics have been confirmed in human stool, lung tissue, and blood [2]. Human exposure occurs mainly through ingestion of contaminated food and water, inhalation of airborne particles, and, to a lesser extent, dermal contact [2].

According to the evidence, microplastics may cause inflammation in the respiratory and gastrointestinal systems and compromise immune function [3]. They may also induce inflammatory responses, oxidative stress, and cellular damage, contributing to various diseases [1]. Possible associations have been reported between microplastics in the body and gastrointestinal complications, inflammatory conditions, hormonal imbalances, and reproductive dysfunction [2]. The combination of microplastics with other environmental pollutants may amplify adverse health outcomes [1].

Overall, human evidence is limited and largely observational, with studies mainly reporting associations between microplastic exposure and selected biological markers rather than confirmed clinical outcomes [2]. Long-term health effects are hard to assess because most studies are short-term or cross-sectional, and there is currently no standardized method to quantify the internal burden of microplastics in humans [2].
